Concept 04

Scheduler

A Pipeline is one workload. A Scheduler is several of them in one process, driven once per tick in the order their dependency edges allow.

In one line
Many pipelines, one dependency-ordered pass per tick
You need
Nothing beyond saci-core. The io feature only changes what a tick does and unlocks the sink-depth probe
Read this if
You have two or more workloads sharing a process, and one of them must wait for another or be skipped because of it

What a Scheduler owns

Three fields: a Vec<Pipeline>, a matching Vec<PipelineConfig>, and a cached stage plan. tick() drives it, and three methods read it back: pipelines(), get(name), get_mut(name).

It owns no shared dataset. Every Pipeline carries its own Dataset, so two pipelines registered with the same scheduler cannot read each other's columns, and a dependency edge between them moves no rows. An edge decides who runs first, and whether the later one runs at all. Nothing else.

Adding pipelines

add_pipeline takes a pipeline and gives it a default PipelineConfig: no dependencies, priority 0, no backpressure. add_pipeline_with_config takes the config explicitly. Both return &mut Self, so calls chain.

Rusttwo ways in, one prelude import
use saci_core::prelude::*;

let mut sched = Scheduler::new();

// Default config: no edges, priority 0, no backpressure.
sched.add_pipeline(
    Pipeline::builder("ingest")
        .with::<Transaction>()
        .with_system(IngestSystem)
        .build(),
);

// Explicit config: one edge, one priority.
sched.add_pipeline_with_config(
    Pipeline::builder("enrich")
        .with::<Transaction>()
        .with_system(EnrichSystem)
        .build(),
    PipelineConfig::new()
        .after("ingest", DependencyKind::Data)
        .priority(-1),
);

PipelineConfig has exactly three fields, one builder method each: dependencies, priority (an i32, lower runs first, default 0), and backpressure (an Option). .after() pushes an edge, so call it once per predecessor. Scheduler, PipelineConfig, DependencyKind and BackpressureSpec are all in saci_core::prelude.

The plan is built once, and cached

The stage plan lives in a OnceLock filled by the first tick(). add_pipeline does not clear it, unlike Pipeline::add_system, which does invalidate its own pipeline's stage cache. Register every pipeline before the first tick. One added afterwards belongs to no stage and will never run, with no error. A bad graph is cached the same way, so a cycle or an unknown dependency name returns the identical error from every later tick.

What one tick does

A tick is one pass over the whole graph. Four steps:

  1. Build the plan, if it is not built yet. build_stages peels the dependency graph with Kahn's algorithm. Every pipeline with no unmet dependency forms stage 1, removing them exposes stage 2, and so on. Each entry in dependencies becomes one edge, and the kind is ignored here, so Order and Data build the same graph. A name that matches no pipeline fails with a message quoting both pipelines, and a cycle fails with "pipeline dependency graph contains a cycle". Either way tick hands it back as a SaciError::Scheduler.
  2. Sort each stage by priority. A stable sort, so pipelines with equal priority keep registration order.
  3. For each member, in that order: test its Data edges, then its backpressure predicate, then run it. The run is run_with_io() when the io feature is on, which drains sources in, runs systems, and drains sinks out. Otherwise it is plain run().
  4. Record whether it produced zero rows, for the Data edges downstream of it.
stages, edges, priority: the plan each pipeline's own Dataset

tick awaits each pipeline before starting the next. Its own doc line reads "run all pipelines sequentially according to the DAG stage plan". Across pipelines, the stage plan buys ordering and the skip semantics below, nothing more.

Concurrency in SACI lives one level down, and even there it is conditional. A stage inside a pipeline means only that nothing orders those systems relative to each other, which is what licenses running them together. They run together, on the tokio + rayon executor, only when every member of that stage implements ParallelSystem, there is more than one of them, and the dataset holds at least 100_000 rows. A stage holding even one plain System, or a smaller dataset, runs its members one at a time, exactly as the scheduler runs a stage of pipelines.

Each pipeline owns its dataset, so two stage-mates share no state to race over. The sequencing is a scheduling choice, and correctness does not rest on it. You drive the cadence yourself.

Rustone tick is one pass; the loop is yours
loop {
    sched.tick().await?;
    tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(250)).await;
}

Order edges and Data edges

Both kinds place the dependent after its predecessor, because build_stages ignores the kind. The difference is entirely at run time, and only Data can cancel a run:

  • DependencyKind::Order: run after the named pipeline, whatever it produced.
  • DependencyKind::Data: run after the named pipeline and skip this tick if that pipeline produced nothing.

"Produced nothing" is a specific condition. A pipeline is flagged as having produced nothing when either:

  • it ran and its last_stats().rows_produced was exactly 0; or
  • it was itself skipped, by one of its own Data edges, or by backpressure.

The second case is what makes chains behave sensibly. A skip propagates down consecutive Data edges, so an idle source does not wake the three stages behind it. An Order edge stops the propagation, because it never consults the flag at all.

rows_produced is a net delta

It is computed as live rows after the run minus live rows before, as an isize. A pipeline that appends 40 rows and soft-deletes 40 nets zero and reads as "produced nothing". A pipeline whose systems only rewrite existing columns always nets zero, so its Data dependents never run. Give those an Order edge instead. Net deletion is not zero, so a shrinking pipeline still wakes its dependents.

Pipeline names are the only identifier an edge has, and nothing checks that they are unique. Register two pipelines under one name and the two halves of the machinery disagree. Edge building resolves the name through a HashMap, which keeps the last registration, while the skip check scans for the first. Keep names unique.

Skips and backpressure

BackpressureSpec has one variant: Predicate(Box<dyn Fn(&Pipeline) -> bool + Send + Sync>). The closure receives the pipeline it gates. Returning true skips that pipeline for the current tick and flags it, so Data dependents skip too. The two checks are ordered. The Data edges are tested first, and a pipeline already skipped is never asked about backpressure.

the scheduler's decisions and flags the run itself, and the rows it netted

The closure is where the io feature earns its place. Pipeline::sink_pending_rows(component) is gated on io and forwards to Sink::pending_rows(), which lets a pipeline pause itself when the sink it writes into has backed up.

Rustpause the writer when its channel fills
use saci_connector_channel::ChannelSink;
use saci_core::prelude::*;

// The receiver is consumed elsewhere; four batches of headroom.
let (sink, rx) = ChannelSink::new(Transaction::schema(), 4);

sched.add_pipeline_with_config(
    Pipeline::builder("ingest")
        .with::<Transaction>()
        .with_system(IngestSystem)
        .with_sink("Transaction", sink)
        .build(),
    PipelineConfig::new().backpressure(BackpressureSpec::Predicate(Box::new(
        |p: &Pipeline| p.sink_pending_rows("Transaction").is_some_and(|n| n >= 10_000),
    ))),
);

Two things about that probe. Sink::pending_rows() returns None by default, so most sinks, file-backed ones included, give the closure nothing to work with. Handle the None deliberately rather than unwrapping it. And ChannelSink answers in rows, as the trait defines it. It tracks the rows it has sent and subtracts the rows the receiver has already taken, so two queued batches of 100 rows read as 200, whatever the channel's slot count is.

Without the io feature the predicate still works, but it has to look at something else. It receives the whole &Pipeline, so last_stats() is available. So is any state you captured in the closure: a clock, an Arc<AtomicBool> flipped by an operator, or a queue depth read from elsewhere in your process.

Errors and cadence

A pipeline's error is returned from tick unchanged, by ?. The rest of that stage does not run, and neither does any later stage. Only plan failures are re-wrapped, as SaciError::Scheduler.

There is no rollback. Pipelines that already ran in that tick kept their effects. Their datasets are mutated and, under io, their sinks have already been written and finished. Systems reached by a retried tick therefore need to be idempotent, exactly as they do under the distributed runner. The next tick starts again from the top of the cached plan, so a pipeline that succeeded before the failure runs a second time.

Nothing is carried between ticks except the plan and each pipeline's own data: the skip flags are a fresh vector per tick. A scheduler with no pipelines ticks successfully and does nothing.

Reading results back

Every pipeline keeps the RunStats from its most recent run, and the scheduler hands you the pipelines themselves, by slice or by name.

Ruststats, and mutation between ticks
// Registration order, not stage order.
for p in sched.pipelines() {
    let s = p.last_stats();
    println!(
        "{:<8} {:>3} systems  {:>6} rows  {:>5} ms  {} retries",
        p.name(), s.systems_run, s.rows_produced, s.duration_millis, s.retries_this_batch,
    );
}

// Feed a pipeline by hand between ticks.
if let Some(p) = sched.get_mut("ingest") {
    p.data_mut().append::<Transaction>(&new_rows)?;
}

A skipped pipeline is not re-run, so its last_stats() still holds the figures from the tick in which it last ran. rows_produced is an isize for that reason. It is a delta, and it can be negative.

When to reach for one

Reach forWhen
One Pipeline One workload over one schema. The pipeline's own stage plan already removes the ordering constraint between independent systems, and a single run() is easier to reason about than a tick.
A Scheduler Several workloads in one process, especially when they use different schemas, different cadences, or must run in a fixed order, such as an ingest pipeline feeding an enrichment pipeline that a report pipeline follows. Also the right tool when one workload should go quiet while another is idle: that is what a Data edge expresses.
The distributed runner One workload that must span several nodes with claim leases, checkpoints and crash recovery. See Distributed processing.

One boundary to know. Scheduler is a saci-core API that you drive from your own binary. saci-service re-exports the type, but a service configuration declares workflows that its own runners drive, and the service never constructs a scheduler. A standalone config may declare several workflows, which run concurrently with no edges between them; cluster mode takes exactly one. Dependency edges, priority and the data-dependency skip are something you write a main for.

That boundary is also where BackpressureSpec::Predicate stops applying. It gates one Pipeline inside a hand-built Scheduler, and a saci-service workflow never constructs a Scheduler at all. What a service workflow gets instead is the runners' own adaptive flow control: an automatic per-source admission target, config-driven rather than a closure, with no predicate to write.
